description: Early lesions are small, light-colored and oval. They form along leaf margins or parallel to the veins, with diffuse, water-soaked edges.
short_quote: "small, light-colored elliptical lesions… diffuse margin and a water-soaked appearance"
source_name: CPN, An Overview of Northern Corn Leaf Blight

description: Lesions keep enlarging up to 6 in (about 15 cm), crossing veins to become typically 'cigar-shaped'. Over time they turn gray to tan.
source_name: CPN Overview NCLB

description: Long elliptical lesions 1–6 in long. Gray-green at first, later light gray or tan.
short_quote: "long (1 to 6 inches) and elliptical, gray-green at first"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Northern Corn Leaf Blight of Corn

description: Relatively large gray or gray-green elliptical to cigar-shaped lesions, 1 in to more than 6 in long, lying parallel to the veins. On some hybrids lesions may have dark borders. Not limited by veins, and no wound is needed for infection.
source_name: Nebraska Extension NebGuide G2270, Northern Corn Leaf Blight (T. A. Jackson-Ziems, 2016)

description: On hybrids with Ht genes, lesions are small and chlorotic and may develop as linear streaks. Such lesions produce few spores.
short_quote: "smaller, chlorotic, and may develop into linear streaks"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia NCLB

description: On hybrids with partial (non-race-specific) resistance, lesions are small, restricted and sporulate little. They appear as narrow yellow or chlorotic streaks rather than cigar shapes and are easily missed.
source_name: CPN Overview NCLB

description: On seed inbreds or some resistant hybrids, lesions may be smaller, more yellow, or produce no spores.
short_quote: "smaller, more yellow, and/or not produce spores"
source_name: NebGuide G2270

description: Lesions may also form on ear husks, but kernels are not infected.
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia NCLB

description: Besides leaves, lesions also form on husks and leaf sheaths.
source_name: NebGuide G2270

description: Under humid conditions dark gray spores form mainly on the **leaf underside**, making lesions look 'dirty gray'.
short_quote: "usually on the lower leaf surface… 'dirty' gray appearance"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia NCLB

description: In the center of mature lesions, dark gray-green spores are borne at the tips of hyphae, not enclosed in other fruiting structures. They can be seen with a hand lens or a smartphone camera at ×20. They are easiest to see after dew or rain and hard to see on dry or old lesions.
short_quote: "dark gray-green spores… not confined within another fungal structure"
source_name: CPN Overview NCLB

description: As lesions mature they turn tan, and spores forming in the middle of the lesion make it look darker and dusty.
source_name: NebGuide G2270

description: In fields with heavy residue it appears first on lower leaves because of spores spread by rain splash and wind. Under suitable conditions it progresses to middle and upper leaves. It may also appear first on upper leaves from windblown spores from neighboring fields. On susceptible hybrids lesions merge and whole leaves dry.
short_quote: "may also be observed first in the upper canopy"
source_name: CPN Overview NCLB
location_in_source: 'When symptoms appear' paragraph; end of 'Symptoms' first paragraph

description: Starts with a few scattered lesions on lower leaves and spreads to upper leaves as favorable conditions continue. One or more lesions form per leaf and enlarge, drying the leaf.
short_quote: "a few lesions scattered in the lower canopy"
source_name: NebGuide G2270

description: Can appear at any time in the season, but is usually observed from the late vegetative stage (V10–V14) to physiological maturity (R6). Under suitable conditions lesions appear within 1 week of infection.
source_name: CPN Overview NCLB

description: Favored by leaf wetness over 6 hours and 18–27 °C (64–81 °F).
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia NCLB

description: Spores need 6–18 hours of water on the leaf surface to germinate. High humidity and mild temperatures are favorable.
short_quote: "6–18 hours of water on the leaf surface"
source_name: NebGuide G2270

description: Conidia are elongated and fusiform with a **protruding hilum**. They have 2–12 septa (most isolates 3–6, 3–7, 3–8 or 3–9). Conidia are 52.94–144.12 µm long and 10.0–25.88 µm wide. Shapes were described as elongated elliptical, obclavate to fusiform, slightly curved (45 isolates from Bihar, India).
source_name: Anwer et al. 2022, Bioengineering 9(8):403 (PMC9405478)
location_in_source: Abstract; 3.1 Cultural and Morphological Characterization; Table 1; Fig. 3

description: Colonies after 10 days on PDA fall into four groups: olive-brown, blackish-brown, whitish-black and gray. Colony forms include flat and cottony-raised, with regular or irregular margins.
short_quote: "olivaceous brown, blackish brown, whitish black, and grayish"
source_name: Anwer et al. 2022

description: β-tubulin gene sequences confirmed isolate identity and phylogenetic relationships.
source_name: Anwer et al. 2022

description: Small pale-brown spots form, with slightly darker brown margins. Lesions spread between veins, and many are about 0.5 cm wide and 1–2 cm long.
source_name: Nongsaro pest information 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)' (RDA)

description: Race T lesions are yellow-brown, 0.6–1.2 cm wide and 0.6–2.7 cm long. They may become fusiform or elliptical with yellow-green or white rings. Race O usually attacks only leaves.
source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

description: Elliptical pale-brown 'sesame-seed spots' 0.5 cm wide and 1–2 cm long form on leaves. As disease intensifies, symptoms enlarge and leaves dry.
source_name: RDA press release "Maize diseases need different control methods by type" (2025-06-16, National Institute of Crop Science)

description: Race O lesions are tan, somewhat rectangular, with reddish-brown borders.
short_quote: "tan, somewhat rectangular in shape… reddish-brown margins"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Southern Corn Leaf Blight of Corn

description: Race T lesions are rectangular to elliptical, ¼–½ in (about 0.6–1.3 cm) wide and ¼–¾ in (about 0.6–1.9 cm) long. There may be a chlorotic zone around the reddish-brown border.
short_quote: "¼ to ½ inch wide by ¼ to ¾ inch long"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia SCLB

description: Lesions vary by race but are generally tan to brown rectangles with brown borders, often with yellow halos. They are smaller than NCLB lesions and stay on lower leaves. They resemble NCLB resistant reaction types, so laboratory diagnosis may be needed.
short_quote: "rectangular lesions with a brown margin… often surrounded by a yellow halo"
source_name: CPN Overview NCLB (section on confusable diseases)
location_in_source: 'Southern corn leaf blight' look-alike subsection, Fig. 10

description: Leaf lesions are brown, sometimes purplish or with reddish-brown borders, occasionally with concentric rings. When they merge they turn gray. Length is 2.5 cm. They are elliptical at first, then elongate lengthwise and become rectangular when limited by veins.
short_quote: "becoming rectangular when spots are restricted by veins"
source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014, "The genus Bipolaris", Studies in Mycology 79:221-288 (PMC4255534)
location_in_source: *Bipolaris maydis* species description, 'Symptoms on Zea mays'

description: Later, race T lesions form on leaves, stalks and sheaths, with dark black to reddish-brown margins. With any race, early leaf infection readily leads to stalk rot.
source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

description: Race T attacks leaves, husks, stalks, sheaths, ear shanks, ears and cobs. Stalk and leaf infections start as purple spots whose centers become tan to gray.
short_quote: "initially appear as purple spots that develop tan-gray centers"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia SCLB

description: Infected kernels can be covered with black mold. Race T causes kernel and ear rot, with large losses in grain and silage yield.
source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

description: When disease is severe, grain and shanks rot.
source_name: RDA press release 2025-06-16

description: When ears are infected, gray-black lesions form on husks and spread to kernels, appearing as black felt-like mold.
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia SCLB

description: Seedlings from infected seed may wilt and die within 3–4 weeks after sowing.
source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

description: Seedlings from infected kernels often wilt.
short_quote: "Seedlings from infected kernels are often blighted"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia SCLB

description: Under suitable conditions, disease development is complete in about 60–72 hours. It overwinters as spores or mycelium in diseased residue, and infected grain is also an important overwintering structure. Primary and secondary spread is by wind and rain splash.
source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

description: Inland it mainly occurs in hot, humid summers (June–August). On Jeju, where planting is early, it may occur in tunnel cultivation due to high temperatures inside the tunnels.
source_name: RDA press release 2025-06-16

description: Damage is great in warm, humid weather at 20–30 °C. Race T occurs more readily than race O in northern areas and is scarce in the dry season with little rain.
source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

description: On normal-cytoplasm maize, race T and race O are hard to distinguish reliably by symptoms. Race T is pathogenic to maize with the Tm-sc gene (T-type male-sterile cytoplasm) and causes smaller lesions on ordinary maize. Race O shows no differential reaction between cytoplasm types.
source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

description: (PDA culture) Conidiophores are (90–)105–470(–712) × 5–7 µm, solitary or in small groups, usually unbranched, septate, olive-brown and geniculate near the top. Conidiogenous nodes are distinctly dark brown.
source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014 (PMC4255534)
location_in_source: *B. maydis* species description 'Asexual morph on PDA', Fig. 22F–I

description: Conidia are (59–)66–102(–160) × (12–)14–18(–20) µm (mean 94 × 16 µm, n=100), pale to medium dark brown, smooth, slightly curved fusiform, with (5–)8(–11) **distosepta**. The hilum is distinct, 3–5 µm wide, and germ tubes arise from both ends of the spore (bipolar). Secondary conidiation is occasionally observed.
source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014

description: Perithecia are (198–)225–459(–600) µm in diameter and black. Ascospores are filiform, 130–340 × 6–9 µm, 5–9-septate and tightly coiled in the ascus (Sach's agar).
source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014

description: Colonies on PDA are grayish-white when young and black when mature.
source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014

description: The Nongsaro page gives only the scientific name (*C. heterostrophus*) and no description of conidia or conidiophores. Morphometrics of Korean isolates: **Unconfirmed**.
source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

description: Early symptoms are brown or tan spots 0.2 in (about 5 mm) wide and 0.4–0.8 in (about 1–2 cm) long filling the space between veins. These lesions become irregular to rectangular, and yellow borders are **easier to see against the light**.
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902, Gray Leaf Spot of Corn

description: Mature lesions are tan or gray, vein-limited rectangles with blunt ends, 0.2 in (about 5 mm) wide and up to 2.8 in (about 7 cm) long. They run parallel to the veins and in severe cases merge, drying the whole leaf.
short_quote: "vein-limited, rectangular-shaped (0.2 inches wide and up to 2.8 inches long), with blunt-ends"
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

description: Lesions are long (up to 2 in), narrow rectangles, light tan, later turning gray. They are usually vein-limited but can merge and kill whole leaves.
short_quote: "long (up to 2 inches), narrow, rectangular, and light tan colored"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Gray Leaf Spot of Corn

description: The typical symptom is tan to brown rectangular lesions on mature leaves, ½–2 in (about 1.3–5 cm) long and 1/8–1/4 in (about 3–6 mm) wide, long and narrow. Secondary and tertiary veins limit their width, so the sides are parallel.
short_quote: "long (1/2 to 2 inches), narrow (1/8 to 1/4 inch), rectangular"
source_name: Purdue Extension BP-56, Gray Leaf Spot of Corn (G. E. Shaner, P. R. Sellers, D. H. Scott)

description: The first symptoms are small, dark, water-soaked spots, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo. The spots enlarge quickly, the central tissue dies, and they elongate into the characteristic long, narrow lesions.
short_quote: "tiny, dark, water-soaked spot… narrow, yellow halo"
source_name: Purdue BP-56

description: *C. zeina* lesions form on both surfaces, are vein-limited, 2–3 mm wide and 5–40 mm long. They merge readily and are pale gray to pale brown, with indistinct borders; young lesions are chlorotic.
short_quote: "Leaf spots amphigenous, vein-limited, 2–3 mm wide, 5–40 mm long"
source_name: Crous et al. 2006, Studies in Mycology 55:189-197 (PMC2104713)

description: *C. zeae-maydis* lesions are oblong and often become elongated streaks or irregular gray to brown spots. Size and shape vary, and narrow brown borders are common.
source_name: Crous et al. 2006

description: Sheath symptoms are relatively large round to oblong tan to dark-brown lesions surrounded by dark-brown to dark-purple borders. They are hard to distinguish from lesions of the NCLB, SCLB and northern corn leaf spot pathogens.
source_name: Purdue BP-56

description: Stalk infection has been reported, and severe cases cause lodging. Sheath and husk lesions may be elliptical and are usually not diagnostic.
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

description: Husk lesions resemble leaf lesions in shape.
short_quote: "Husk lesions are similar in appearance to leaf lesions"
source_name: Purdue BP-56

description: Gray spores emerge from mature lesions, which is the origin of the disease name.
short_quote: "release of gray fungal spores… gives the disease its name"
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

description: Lesions are tan at first and take on a gray color when many spores form on the lesion surface.
short_quote: "may become grayish when the fungus produces numerous spores"
source_name: Purdue BP-56

description: Up to 5,000 conidia form per mm² of a typical lesion, of which 50–80% can germinate.
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

description: Conidiophore fascicles (caespituli) form on both surfaces but mainly on the leaf underside. They are punctiform to slightly spreading and brown.
source_name: Crous et al. 2006

description: Stromata in overwintered residue produce conidia, which reach the lower leaves of the new crop by wind and rain splash. They enter through stomata within 4–7 days, and chlorosis appears about 9 days after infection. Secondary conidia form 14–21 days after inoculation. The infection cycle is 14–21 days on susceptible hybrids and 21–28 days on tolerant hybrids.
short_quote: "Chlorotic symptoms can develop in about nine days"
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

description: Tolerant hybrids produce chlorotic or fleck-type lesions, while susceptible hybrids produce elongated necrotic lesions.
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

description: Symptoms first appear on lower leaves about 2–3 weeks before tasseling.
short_quote: "first appear on lower leaves about two to three weeks before tasseling"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia GLS

description: Under favorable conditions symptoms usually appear 2–4 weeks before pollination.
short_quote: "two to four weeks prior to pollination"
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

description: Requires at least 12 hours of free moisture and RH of 90% or above. The original gives temperature as '70–90 °F/25–32 °C' (70 °F is about 21 °C, so the conversion is wrong).
short_quote: "at least 12 hours of free moisture… ≥90 percent"
source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

description: Infection and development are favored by warm weather (80s °F) and humid weather with RH of 90% or above lasting more than 12 hours.
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia GLS

description: Conidiophores emerge through stomata in fascicles of 3–14, 40–180 × 4–8 µm, with (0–)1–8 septa, pale olive to medium brown and geniculate. Conidiogenous loci are thickened and darkened, 2–3 µm wide. Conidia are solitary, broadly obclavate to subcylindrical, 30–100 × 4–9 µm, 1–10-septate and hyaline. The apex is obtuse and the base obconically truncate, with a slightly thickened, darkened hilum 2–3 µm wide.
source_name: Crous et al. 2006

description: Conidiophores form loose fascicles of 3–20, 40–100 × 5–7 µm, 1–5-septate. Conidiogenous cells are 40–60 × 5–6 µm, and loci are thickened, darkened, refractive and 2–3 µm wide. Conidia are broadly fusiform, (40–)60–75(–100) × (6–)7–8(–9) µm, (1–)3–5(–10)-septate and hyaline, with a thickened, darkened hilum 2–3 µm wide.
source_name: Crous et al. 2006

description: *C. zeae-maydis*: colonies 15–25 mm in diameter after 3 weeks on PDA; on OA the surface turns red (red cercosporin pigment). *C. zeina*: grows more slowly, 10–15 mm after 3 weeks on PDA, with no red pigment. On MEA both species are olive-gray with iron-gray reverse.
source_name: Crous et al. 2006
location_in_source: 'Cultural characteristics' and Notes for both species

description: Conidial sizes of the two species are similar. *C. zeae-maydis* has longer conidiophores (up to 180 µm vs 100 µm) and obclavate conidia, while *C. zeina* has fusiform conidia. Species are separated by culture growth rate, red pigment and multigene sequencing.
source_name: Crous et al. 2006

description: The RDA 2025 press release describes 'jeommunui-byeong' (leaf spot) as gray to yellow-brown rectangular symptoms on leaves, sometimes with yellow round dot-like symptoms. It says the disease was rare in Korea in the past but is now spreading. **With no scientific name given, whether it is the same disease as GLS is Unconfirmed**.
source_name: RDA press release 2025-06-16
source_type: Korean official (match to disease name unconfirmed)

description: Appears mainly on leaves. Diseased leaves become mottled and senesce. Yellow to orange 'aecia' (as worded in the source) form on the leaf **underside**, and small yellow to yellowish-white lesions form on the surface of lower leaves.
short_quote: "yellow to orange aecia (as worded) form on the leaf underside" (translated from Korean)
source_name: Nongsaro pest information 'Rust (銹病, Rust)' (pathogen *Puccinia sorghi*; crop not named)

description: The first symptom is chlorotic flecks on the leaf surface. Soon spores break through the epidermis to form powdery brick-red pustules.
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Common Rust of Corn

description: Pustules are oval or elongated, about 1/8 in (about 3 mm) long. They occur sparsely scattered or in clusters. Tissue around pustules yellows or dies, forming necrotic lesions, sometimes as bands across the leaf. With age the red spores turn black so pustules look black.
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust

description: Yellow spots quickly develop into oval to elongated reddish-brown powdery pustules. Pustules rupture the epidermis so leaves look bumpy. Pustules are usually 1/8 in long, single or in groups, with torn epidermis around them. Dark reddish-brown pustules are scattered on **both upper and lower leaf surfaces** and turn dark brown to black with age.
short_quote: "scattered over both the upper and lower surfaces" (Fig. 1 caption)
source_name: Cornell Vegetables, Common Rust of Sweet Corn (Cornell University)

description: Common rust pustules are raised, brick-red to brown, turn black with age, and spores rub off. They are less dense than southern rust. They form on **both leaf surfaces** and are abundant in the lower to middle canopy. No chlorotic halo is described.
source_name: CPN, An Overview of Southern Rust (CPN-2009, 2019)
location_in_source: Table 1; 'Southern rust vs. common rust' section; Fig. 7

description: On Korean *P. sorghi* specimens, uredinia and telia appeared on **both upper and lower leaf surfaces**. Uredinia are reddish-brown and oblong (Results 3.1), summarized in the Discussion as 'circular uredinia'. Telia are blackish-brown, fusiform to linear.
short_quote: "Uredinia and telia appeared on both adaxial and abaxial leaf surfaces"
source_name: Lee YK et al. 2025, Mycobiology 53(5):637-647 (PMC12337728)

description: Husks, sheaths and stalks can also be infected. Pustules also form on the leaf midrib (photo caption).
short_quote: "Husks, leaf sheaths, and stalks also may be infected"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust
location_in_source: Body first paragraph; photo caption 'on leaf midrib'

description: (US Midwest) Pustules usually first appear in late June.
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust

description: Often starts at the late vegetative stage (southern rust after VT).
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

description: The 4 Korean *P. sorghi* specimens are 3 from Gangwon (1992) and 1 from Jeonbuk (2021), all collected in late autumn (October–November).
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Favored by high humidity, daytime temperatures of 60–77 °F and night temperatures of 65–70 °F. Leaves must be wet for at least 3 hours for infection. In New York it does not overwinter and blows in from the south each year. In the tropics and subtropics it completes its life cycle on the alternate host *Oxalis*.
short_quote: "requires leaves to be wet for at least 3 hours"
source_name: Cornell Common Rust

description: Urediniospores from Korean specimens are globose to subglobose or ovoid and **brown**, 22–35 × 23–34 µm (mean 29 × 26 µm, n=30), with echinulate walls.
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Teliospores from Korean specimens are oblong or obovoid, 31–40 × 18–26 µm (mean 36 × 21 µm, n=100).
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Common rust spores are brick-red, while southern rust spores are more orange (photo caption).
short_quote: "Common rust spores… brick red… southern rust spores… more orange"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust

description: Common rust spores are darker and rounder; southern rust spores are lighter and slightly elongated.
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

description: A heteroecious rust fungus requiring *Oxalis* species as the alternate host. Under favorable conditions it is associated with 18–49% yield loss.
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Phylogenetic analysis of ITS, LSU rDNA and COX3 mtDNA separates it into a clade distinct from *P. polysora*. For old specimens only ITS1 was amplified with PsorF/PsorR.
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Pustules are orange to tan, round or oval, about 1/16 in (1.5 mm) in diameter. Most form on the **upper** leaf surface, and usually only chlorosis is seen on the underside. Rubbed spores leave orange to tan streaks on fingers or clothing.
short_quote: "Most pustules form on the upper surface" (gist)
source_name: CPN, An Overview of Southern Rust (Bradley et al., CPN-2009, 2019-08-01)

description: Secondary-infection pustules are very numerous and dense. Light green to yellow chlorotic halos are common and visible on the leaf underside.
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

description: Symptoms resemble common rust, but pustules are smaller and form **almost only on the upper leaf surface**. They are usually round or oval, very numerous and densely scattered over the leaf surface. Spores are orange when they erupt. With age pustules turn chocolate-brown to black and may form dark rings around the original pustules.
short_quote: "occur almost exclusively on the upper leaf surface"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Southern Rust of Corn

description: On Korean specimens, uredinial symptoms appeared on **both upper and lower leaf surfaces** and rarely on stalks. Uredinia are oval or round, varying from yellow to brown. Systemic infection and chlorotic lesions were also observed as field symptoms.
short_quote: "Uredinial symptoms appeared on both adaxial and abaxial leaf surfaces"
source_name: Lee YK et al. 2025, Mycobiology 53(5):637-647 (PMC12337728)

description: In Korean field surveys, *P. polysora* often formed uredinia on both leaf surfaces like *P. sorghi*. Therefore an earlier poster report (Gunwi) that identified southern rust only from upper-surface predominance has limited reliability.
short_quote: "often formed uredinia on both leaf surfaces, similar to P. sorghi"
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Uredinia on Michigan (USA) specimens are mainly clustered on the upper leaf surface. They are pale cinnamon-brown to bright orange, ovoid and surrounded by yellow halos.
short_quote: "aggregated primarily on the upper leaf surface"
source_name: "First Report of Southern Rust (Puccinia polysora) on Corn (Zea mays) in Michigan", Plant Disease (2022) — AGRIS abstract

description: Pustules on specimens from Tianjin, China are randomly scattered on leaves, cinnamon to tan. They were found mainly on upper leaves and rarely on ear husks. No teliospores were found.
source_name: Liu X et al. 2018, Plant Disease 102(4):826 "Occurrence of Puccinia polysora… Northeast Huanghuaihai Region of China" — AGRIS abstract

description: Old pustules may become brown to black telia. They resemble tar spot perithecia, so laboratory confirmation may be needed.
short_quote: "Later in the season, the fungus forms darker pustules called telia" (encyclopedia caption)
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust; CPN Encyclopedia Southern Rust
location_in_source: 'Symptoms and Signs', Fig. 2; encyclopedia photo caption

description: In severe cases pustules also form on husks, leaf sheaths and ear shanks.
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

description: Pustules usually first appear in the middle to upper canopy, often starting in isolated hot spots near field ends or edges. Under favorable conditions the time from infection to sporulation can be as short as 9 days, and one pustule sporulates for up to 8 days. Young leaves are more susceptible than mature leaves.
short_quote: "first observed in the middle or upper plant canopy"
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

description: Usually appears after tasseling (VT). Late-planted or double-cropped maize is at greater risk.
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

description: The 33 Korean *P. polysora* specimens (Gangwon 2, Chungbuk 2, Chungnam 3, Jeonbuk 23, Jeonnam 3) were mainly collected in September and October (2021–2024).
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Infection can occur after about 6 hours of leaf wetness, and dew is often enough. High relative humidity and about 80 °F (27 °C) are favorable. It needs living green tissue and cannot overwinter in the north.
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

description: Urediniospore germination was highest at 25 °C (49%) and similar at 20–30 °C. It fell sharply above 32 °C and was under 2% at 38 and 40 °C. At 25–28 °C more than 40% germinated within 9 hours.
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Urediniospores are light brown, ellipsoid or subglobose, 25–40 × 17–29 µm (mean 33 × 24 µm, n=30), with **hyaline echinulate walls**.
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Urediniospores are yellow to golden in the center and hyaline along the outer membrane, ellipsoid to obovoid with short echinulations (light microscope ×40), 17–28 × 26–38 µm (n=180). Telia were not observed. Identity was confirmed by 28S rDNA.
short_quote: "hyaline along the outer membrane, ellipsoid to obovoid"
source_name: Plant Disease 2022 Michigan new record (AGRIS abstract)

description: Urediniospores are yellowish, subglobose or globose, yellow to golden, 25.0–30.0 × 28.0–37.0 µm, with echinulate surfaces. No teliospores were found.
short_quote: "subglobose or globose showing yellow or golden color"
source_name: Liu et al. 2018, Plant Disease (AGRIS abstract)

description: The text says telia were not observed on Korean specimens. However, the Fig. 2(P) caption reads "SEM image of telia", so there is an **internal inconsistency in the paper**.
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Since the uredinial and telial stages have been observed only on maize and no alternate host is known, it may be autoecious, but this is not confirmed.
short_quote: "plausible that the species exhibits an autoecious life cycle"
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Phylogenetic analysis of ITS, LSU rDNA and COX3 mtDNA separates it into a clade distinct from *P. sorghi*. This study is the first to use COX3 for phylogenetic analysis of maize rusts.
source_name: Lee et al. 2025

description: Southern rust can be confirmed in the diagnostic lab by identifying *P. polysora* spores under the microscope.
source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

description: Occurs mainly on ears, stalks and leaves, and rarely on roots. Diseased parts enlarge into galls.
source_name: Nongsaro pests by crop: maize Common smut (D00001177)

description: Large galls are 10 cm or more in diameter. They are covered at first by a glossy white membrane, and when the membrane bursts, black powdery chlamydospores are released.
source_name: Nongsaro D00001177

description: Overwintered chlamydospores germinate to produce sporidia, which are carried by wind and enter tender tissue. Galls are produced only by hyphae formed by fusion of sporidia of different mating types. The latent period is 7–21 days.
source_name: Nongsaro D00001177

category: Symptoms - whole plant / timing of occurrence
description: Any aerial part is attacked from seedling to maturity, which distinguishes it from other grass smuts. It is most common on young, actively growing plants wounded by detasseling, hail, blowing soil, insects or machinery.
short_quote: "any part of the plant above ground may be attacked"
source_name: Univ. Illinois RPD No. 203 *Corn Smuts* (1990)

category: Symptoms - ear/grain / Symptoms - tassel / Symptoms - stalk
description: All actively growing or embryonic tissue is susceptible. Galls are common on tassels, husks, ears and kernels, stalks, leaves and axillary buds, and rare on aerial roots.
short_quote: "All actively growing or embryonic corn tissue is susceptible."
plant_part: Tassel, husks, ear, kernels, stalk, leaves, axillary buds
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: As galls enlarge they are covered by a shiny greenish-white to silvery-white membrane, and the interior darkens as spores form. Mature galls reach 15 cm (6 in) in diameter. They are filled with dark olive-brown to black, oily to powdery spores. At maturity the white outer membrane bursts and spores are released.
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Small, hard, pea-sized galls form on leaves. Unlike large galls, these are not spore masses. Leaf galls and galls at detasseling wounds are usually small and cause little damage.
short_quote: "small, hard, pea-sized galls that form on the leaves"
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Plants with galls on the lower stalk become sterile or bear several small ears. In autumn they look red, resembling aphid-damaged plants. Yield loss is greatest when large galls are on or above the ear.
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Chlamydospores are diploid, black, globose to subglobose and echinulate, 8–12 µm in diameter. At 10–35 °C with moisture they produce a four-celled basidium (promycelium), on which four or more ovoid sporidia of two mating types (+)/(−) form.
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Hyphae inside galls grow between cells until just before sporulation. They then invade and break down the enlarged host cells. A completed gall consists mainly of dikaryotic hyphae and host cell remnants, and only the membrane enclosing the gall is unaffected by the fungus.
short_quote: "Only the membrane covering the smut gall is unaffected"
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: From infection to a mature gall takes one to several weeks under suitable conditions. Spores from the first galls can reinfect the same or other plants. Gall formation and spore dispersal are almost continuous throughout the summer growing season. Ears are infected by hyphae growing along the silks.
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Infection is most severe when early-season rainfall is low and temperatures are 26–34 °C (79–93 °F). Dry periods that slow growth, and unusually cool, humid weather that slows young plants, also favor infection.
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Galls form on stalks, leaves, ears and tassels, and actively growing tissue is especially susceptible. Galls are swollen, distorted growths, covered at first by a shiny white membrane. When the membrane bursts, a blackish-brown to black powdery spore mass is exposed.
source_name: Crop Protection Network (CPN) Encyclopedia: Common Smut of Corn

description: Excess nitrogen and manure, herbicide injury, mechanical wounds, and relatively dry, warm weather favor disease. No figures are given.
source_name: CPN Common Smut

category: Symptoms - ear/grain (differentiation from other ear rots)
description: Kernels grow into gray tumor-like fungal masses (galls) with black spores inside, which burst when dry to release spores. Ear-rot fungi can mummify kernels or cover them with sooty spores but do not form galls. The common smut fungus forms galls on any part, including brace roots, leaves, stalks and tassels.
source_name: CPN-2001 *An Overview of Ear Rots* (2024 revision)

description: The List of Plant Diseases in Korea (2004) records "smut caused by *Ustilago zeae*" as a fungal disease occurring in Korea (secondary citation in the paper's introduction).
source_name: Han et al. 2015, *Res. Plant Dis.* 21(4):280-289 (paper on biocontrol of stalk rot)

description: The disease is not apparent until tassels and ears emerge.
short_quote: "not evident until the tassels and ears appear"
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Sori form on tassels and ears, and rarely on leaves. Sori are compact masses of blackish-brown to black chlamydospores, covered by a thin grayish-white membrane that soon ruptures. The powdery spores are quickly dispersed by wind and rain.
short_quote: "covered with a thin grayish white membrane which soon ruptures"
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Tangled thread-like strands, remnants of the inflorescence vascular tissue, extend among the sori. This is characteristic of the disease. Vascular strands surrounded by blackish-brown spore masses distinguish it from common smut.
short_quote: "vascular strands... distinguishes head smut from common smut"
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Infected tassels are wholly or partly covered by sori and usually produce no pollen. Individual florets are completely replaced by chlamydospores without gall formation. Gall formation is characteristic of common smut.
short_quote: "replaced entirely by teliospores without the formation of a gall"
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Leaf-like and husk-like structures proliferate from the ear (phyllody). Streaks filled with chlamydospores form on leaves.
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Chlamydospores are diploid, reddish-brown to black, globose to subglobose, with many prominent spines, 9–14 µm in diameter. In soil they directly produce dikaryotic infection hyphae or form basidia. Sporidia are unicellular, haploid, hyaline and subglobose, 7–15 µm.
short_quote: "reddish brown to black, globose to subglobose, abundantly and conspicuously spiny"
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Sporidia of compatible mating types fuse to form infection hyphae that infect seedlings. Hyphae spread systemically into the seedling meristem, then into undifferentiated ear and tassel tissue, converting part or all of it into sori. Chlamydospores in soil survive 3 years or more.
growth_stage: Infection at seedling stage, expression at flowering
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: Low soil moisture (15–25% w/w) is optimal for seedling infection (part of the original sentence is garbled). Temperature is more important than soil moisture for infection. It is more common in clay loam than in sandy or silt loam and worse with nitrogen deficiency.
source_name: Illinois RPD 203

description: The 'galls' on tassels and ears are at first covered by a thin tissue layer that then ruptures, exposing black spore masses and thread-like vascular remnants. Leafy proliferation occurs on tassels and ears.
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia: Head Smut of Corn

description: Ears may degenerate and be replaced by proliferating leaf tissue, and plants may be severely stunted. There is a photo caption showing ear tissue replaced by leafy proliferation and spore masses.
short_quote: "Ears may be aborted and replaced with a proliferation of leafy tissue."
source_name: CPN Head Smut

description: Ears and tassels are replaced by sori filled with chlamydospores. Tassels show wire-like vascular protrusions, and ears show finger-like proliferation. Infected ears are teardrop-shaped, lack silks, and are filled with chlamydospores inside the husks.
short_quote: "wire-like extensions of the vascular bundles in the tassel"
source_name: Univ. Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch: Head Smut

description: The fungus survives as thick-walled black chlamydospores. Unlike common smut, the chlamydospores are not inside fleshy galls. Infection is systemic from the seedling stage but becomes evident only on flowering plants. Infected ears and tassels are usually sterile.
growth_stage: Infection at seedling stage, expression at flowering
source_name: UNL CropWatch

category: Symptoms - tassel / Symptoms - ear/grain / Symptoms - leaf
description: Sporulation sites are tassels, ears and rarely leaves. The galls are rough and, when ruptured, expose dry spore masses mixed with strands of vascular tissue. Usually the whole ear is replaced by spores, but some ears bear a few kernels. Tassels are wholly or partly infected, sometimes limited to spikelets or proliferating into bizarre leaf-like structures.
short_quote: "dry spore masses with strands of vascular tissue"
source_name: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Corn – Head Smut

description: In some hybrids stunting is the main symptom. Ears degenerate, or only a vestige bearing leafy buds remains instead of a normal ear. If only the ear is infected, the tassel is sterile.
short_quote: "Dwarfing may be a dominant symptom in some varieties."
source_name: PNW Handbook

description: Spores survive in soil for at least 5–7 years. Infection is said to occur at the seedling stage, but greenhouse studies found infection even several weeks after sowing. After infection it spreads systemically. Infection occurs even at a soil temperature of 15 °C (59 °F) and more readily at 20–30 °C (68–86 °F). It is not transmitted inside seed but can be carried on the seed surface.
growth_stage: Seedling stage to several weeks after sowing
source_name: PNW Handbook

category: Symptoms - tassel / Symptoms - leaf / Symptoms - whole plant (overseas original paper)
description: Introduction: tassels and ears are partly or completely replaced by 'large white galls containing blackish-brown spores', with stunting, loss of apical dominance and increased tillering. Results: tassel symptom types differ by line: (A) the whole tassel is charred, showing black threads and abundant spores; (B) spore-free leafy clustered structures form; (C) spores only at the base. Chlorotic spots appear on leaves at VE–V8.
growth_stage: VE-V8 (leaf spots), V12-VT (period when tassel symptoms are determined)
source_name: Wang et al. 2024, *Plants* 13(2):238 (China)

description: Incidence in northern China is 7–35%, up to 80% in some areas (cited in the introduction). The resistant line Mo17 averaged 1.5% over 5 years, while susceptible Huangzao4 averaged 88.7%.
source_name: Wang et al. 2024

description: Gives the forma specialis name "*Sporisorium reilianum* f.sp. *zeae* (Kühn) Langdon and Fullerton" for the head smut pathogen of maize and sorghum (PubMed abstract).
source_name: Sabbagh et al. 2008, *Commun. Agric. Appl. Biol. Sci.* 73(2):101-8 (PMID 19226747)

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: Early on, ear husks and kernels are partly pink or reddish-brown. As it progresses, pinkish mold grows in cottony clumps on kernels and husks.
source_name: Nongsaro pests by crop: Ear rot (D00001173)

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: Mold grows especially around insect holes and wounds. With late infection, white streaks may form on the kernel pericarp.
source_name: Nongsaro D00001173

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: Common in warm, slightly dry weather. It occurs mainly on ears wounded or bored by birds or insects rather than healthy ears. Susceptibility of Korean cultivars is not well known. It also occurs during storage.
source_name: Nongsaro D00001173

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: Diseased kernels are scattered on the ear or clustered. They are especially common on kernels damaged by European corn borer, corn earworm and birds. Kernels turn purple, tan or brown. When mold is visible it is white to pink or purple.
short_quote: "Diseased kernels are scattered or in patches on the ear"
source_name: CPN-2001 *An Overview of Ear Rots* (2024 revision)

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: White streaks may form on kernels, called the 'starburst' symptom. It results from the pathogen growing beneath the kernel pericarp (seed coat).

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: The fungus survives on crop residue and spreads readily by windborne spores. It infects seedlings and developing kernels and can grow in stalks and ears for a time without symptoms or signs. Airborne conidia infect via silks or insect wounds, and soilborne conidia via roots. White to pink or purple cottony mold can form anywhere on the ear.

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: Occurs in many environments, but the most severe outbreaks are in warm areas and in fields with heavy insect or hail damage. Fumonisin levels rise when wet, warm weather continues just before harvest. Fumonisin levels can be high even when disease does not look severe. Table 1 gives the conditions as 'moderate to warm temperatures at silking, wet period before harvest'.
short_quote: "fumonisin concentration... can be high even when the disease does not appear to be severe"

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: The only reliable way to confirm ear rot or mycotoxins is often laboratory testing. If unsure, submit samples for laboratory diagnosis. Scouting starts at late dent (R5).
short_quote: "A lab test is often the only reliable way"

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: The most common ear disease, caused by several *Fusarium* species. White to pink or salmon-colored cottony mold forms on one or several kernels, scattered or in clusters. Rot often starts at insect-damaged kernels, and infected kernels are tan or brown or have white streaks.
short_quote: "white to pink or salmon-colored, cottony mold"
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia: Fusarium Ear Rot of Corn

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: The causal fungi overwinter in maize residue and dead grass weeds. Spores reach silks by wind and rain splash and also infect through kernel wounds made by insects and others. Insects also act as vectors. *F. verticillioides* can grow throughout the plant and may reach the ear via the stalk. High temperature and dryness at and after silking are favorable.
source_name: CPN Fusarium Ear Rot

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: White to peach or purple cottony mold forms on one or several kernels scattered over the whole ear. Infected kernels are tan or brown or show starburst white streaks. Symptoms vary with genotype, weather and severity. In severe cases the ear is almost consumed, and the lightened husks are bound to the kernels by mycelium.
source_name: Univ. Tennessee UT Crops: Fusarium Ear Rot (H.M. Kelly)

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: Occurs under a wide range of weather conditions, but is most severe with temperatures above 25 °C (77 °F) and a wet period before harvest. Infection occurs at silking, but spread continues after R6 until grain moisture falls below 18%. The optimum temperature for fumonisin production is 75 °F (about 24 °C).
source_name: UT Crops

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: The most common causal fungi are *F. verticillioides*, *F. proliferatum* and *F. subglutinans*. Of these, *F. verticillioides* and *F. proliferatum* are associated with fumonisin production.
source_name: UT Crops

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: The maize pathogen *F. verticillioides* produces abundant, mostly single-celled microconidia in characteristic long chains by enteroblastic phialidic conidiogenesis.
short_quote: "mostly single-celled microconidia in distinctive long chains"
source_name: Glenn, Richardson & Bacon 2004, *Mycologia* 96(5):968-80 (PMID 21148918)

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: Microconidia of *F. verticillioides* occur in two forms, chains and false heads. In mutants lacking the hydrophobin genes *HYD1* and *HYD2*, chains were rare and almost only false heads formed. That is, chain formation is a trait that can change at the gene level.
source_name: Fuchs, Czymmek & Sweigard 2004, *Fungal Genet. Biol.* 41(9):852-64

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
category: Pathogen morphology (comparison table; soil isolates, not maize)
description: *F. verticillioides*: microconidia are ovoid, aseptate, in long chains of more than 20. Macroconidia are slender, 3–5-septate and rare. Conidiogenous cells are monophialides, and there are no chlamydospores. Pigment is white to dark or pale purple. *F. proliferatum*: microconidia vary in shape and form chains of 11–15. Monophialides and polyphialides occur together, and false heads also form. No chlamydospores; pigment white to pale violet.
source_name: Karim et al. 2016, *Trop. Life Sci. Res.* 27(1):1-20 (isolates from Malaysian peat soil)

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: *F. temperatum* isolated from ear-rot ears (pink or white mold) in Jilin, China: colonies on PDA are white and cottony at first, becoming pinkish-white. Microconidia are hyaline, 0–2-septate, obovoid to ovoid and do not form chains. No chlamydospores. Macroconidia are falcate, 3–5-septate (mostly 4) with a foot-shaped basal cell. Identification was confirmed by TEF-1α sequence (100% match).
source_name: Zhang et al. 2014, *Plant Dis.* 98(9):1273 (First Report, China)

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: In 2011–2015, 878 FFSC isolates were obtained from Korean grains (barley, maize, rice, soybean) and identified by TEF-1α and RPB2 sequences. In maize, *F. verticillioides* 33.9%, *F. fujikuroi* 25.3% and *F. proliferatum* 21.1% dominated. All isolates of *F. fujikuroi*, *F. proliferatum*, *F. verticillioides* and *F. thapsinum* were *FUM1*-positive. Of 19 *F. fujikuroi* isolates, 16 produced more than 1000 µg/g fumonisin (FB1+FB2) on rice medium.
source_name: Choi et al. 2018, *Int. J. Food Microbiol.* 267:62-69 (RDA National Institute of Agricultural Sciences)

scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
description: The List of Plant Diseases in Korea (2004) records ear rot caused by *Gibberella fujikuroi* and stalk rot caused by *F. moniliforme*. The *G. fujikuroi* species complex, formerly called *F. moniliforme*, has been shown to be a species complex of several species. Korean stalk-rot isolates were identified as *F. subglutinans* and *F. temperatum* by morphology and EF1α sequencing (stalk rot, not ear rot).
source_name: Han et al. 2015, *Res. Plant Dis.* 21(4):280-289

description: Occurs on ears at harvest and during storage. At harvest, infection mainly starts at the ear tip, discoloring and rotting inward. During storage, kernels discolor and rot at any part of the ear.
source_name: Nongsaro maize pest document 'Red mold disease (Gibberella)' (attached doc, kidofcomdtyNo=29198)

category: Symptoms - ear/grain / signs (husks adhering, red color)
description: Severely diseased ears rot entirely together with the husks. Abundant pink to red mycelium and spore masses form between husks and ear. During storage, white mycelium covers the seed and later pink to red conidial masses form. Severe ears turn red overall and rot. Eating it causes poisoning in pigs and other livestock.
source_name: Nongsaro Gibberella (red mold) disease document

description: Produces ascospores, conidia and chlamydospores. In nature the ascigerous stage is rare and mainly conidia are produced. No microconidia, only macroconidia. Macroconidia are sickle-blade-shaped, 3–7-septate, 25–62 × 2.5–5.0 µm. Chlamydospores are hyaline to pale brown, globose, 10–12 µm in diameter.
source_name: Nongsaro Gibberella (red mold) disease document

description: Optimum growth temperature is 24–26 °C. No description of colony pigment (Unconfirmed).
source_name: Nongsaro Gibberella (red mold) disease document

description: Overwinters as asci, conidia and mycelium on diseased ears and husks, then causes primary infection. Lesions produce conidia again for secondary infection. Disease starts at silk formation and continues through harvest into storage. Frequent rain at silk formation favors infection and severe disease.
source_name: Nongsaro Gibberella (red mold) disease document

description: Pinkish mold often starts at the ear tip. On severe ears the mold binds the husks and silks tightly to the ear, called 'mummified ears'. Unless the hybrid is highly susceptible or conditions extreme, only part of the ear is attacked.
short_quote: "pinkish mold that often begins at the ear tip"
source_name: CPN-2001 *An Overview of Ear Rots* (2024 revision)

description: Relatively easy to recognize in the field on intact ears, but much harder after shelling. DON or zearalenone levels can be high even when disease does not look severe.
short_quote: "much more difficult to identify after the grain has been shelled"

description: Overwinters on maize and small-grain residue and can also infect soybean roots. Spores produced on residue cause infection at silking. Rain splash and spores discharged from special structures infect via silks or the ear base. More common when cool and wet at early silking. Worse when autumn rains delay harvest. Most severe in continuous-maize fields and areas with wheat head blight. Table 1 summarizes the conditions as 'cool, wet' and the symptom as 'pink to white mycelial growth'.
short_quote: "Red or pink mold forms, typically beginning at the ear tip."
location_in_source: 'Gibberella Ear Rot' paragraphs 2-3, Figure 7 caption, Table 1

description: Most easily recognized by the red or pink color of the mold. Almost always starts at the ear tip. With heavy mold, silks and husks stick to the ear, and in severe cases pink mold is visible on the outside of the husks at the ear tip. A photo of disease on a hail-damaged ear is included.
short_quote: "It almost always begins at the tip of the ear."
source_name: CPN Encyclopedia: Gibberella Ear Rot of Corn

description: The fungus overwinters on maize residue, and spores spread by rain splash and wind to infect via silks. Silks are most susceptible 2–6 days after emergence. Common when cool and wet during grain fill.
short_quote: "Silks are most susceptible two to six days after emergence."
source_name: CPN Gibberella Ear Rot

description: The fungus infects mainly through the silk channel, producing pinkish-white mold at the ear tip. Cool, wet weather (rain or high relative humidity) during and after silking (R1) is optimal. The same pathogen also causes stalk rot and wheat head blight.
short_quote: "pinkish-white mold to develop at the tip of the ear"
source_name: Ohio State Univ. Fact Sheet AC-52 (Willyerd, Paul, Mills, Thomison)

description: Kernels with similar visible mold can differ in internal colonization and toxin production. Kernels that look healthy can also be contaminated. Black light cannot detect vomitoxin, which does not fluoresce. ELISA is toxin-specific, so zearalenone and aflatoxin need separate tests. A rule of thumb is not to feed grain with more than 5% moldy kernels.
source_name: OSU AC-52

description: Pink to red mold starts at the ear tip and progresses toward the base. Pinkish mold is generally diagnostic of this disease. Severe ears are mostly rotted with husks and silks tightly bound, and pink to red mold may grow between husks and ear. Except in highly susceptible hybrids, only part of the ear is attacked.
short_quote: "begins at the tip of the ear and develops toward the base"
growth_stage: Just before harvest (best time for scouting)
source_name: Purdue Extension BP-77-W *Gibberella Ear Rot* (Woloshuk & Wise)
location_in_source: p.1 'Scouting and Identifying', Figures 1-2; p.2 first paragraph

description: Common when cool and wet during the first 21 days after silking. At grain moisture above 22% and about 80 °F, fungal growth and toxin production continue inside the ear. Cold periods below 50 °F can increase zearalenone production. Spread and toxin accumulation stop when grain moisture falls below 18%. The presence and amount of DON can be determined only by chemical analysis.
short_quote: "Only a chemical analysis can verify the presence and amount of" DON
source_name: Purdue BP-77-W
location_in_source: p.1 introduction; p.2 'Mycotoxin Testing'; p.3 'Minimizing Economic Losses'

description: The sexual stage of *G. zeae* forms purple to black perithecia, a distinguishing feature of the genus *Gibberella*. Ascospores are usually 3-septate, slightly shorter and thicker than conidia, without a foot cell. No microconidia; only one type, macroconidia. Macroconidia are banana-shaped, 3-septate when mature, with the foot cell typical of *Fusarium*. Conidial masses are pink. (Description centered on wheat head blight)
short_quote: "produces only one kind of conidia - macroconidia"
source_name: Hallen & Volk, Tom Volk's Fungus of the Month (Univ. Wisconsin–La Crosse; aug2005 page)

category: Pathogen (Korean FGSC composition; molecular, toxin type)
description: 568 *F. graminearum* isolates from maize at 8 Korean locations were analyzed by AFLP, identifying lineages 2, 3, 6 and 7. Proportions were lineage 7 75%, 6 12%, 3 12%, 2 1%. Sexual fertility (female fertility) was lineage 7 100%, 6 70%, 3 26%, 2 14%. All lineage 3 and 7 isolates produced DON, while most lineage 2 and 6 isolates produced NIV.
source_name: Lee et al. 2012, *Appl. Environ. Microbiol.* 78(7):2161-7 (PMC3302601)

description: FGSC isolates from ear rot in Chongqing, China were divided by TEF-1α sequence into 16 *F. meridionale* and 3 *F. asiaticum* isolates. Identification was based on 'morphological and molecular' results, with TEF-1α sequences analyzed when species-specific PCR was inconclusive.
source_name: Zhou et al. 2018, *Toxins* 10(2):90 (China)

description: The List of Plant Diseases in Korea (2004) records it as "red mold disease caused by *G. zeae* (Gibberella stalk rot)" (secondary citation). The English name is given as stalk rot.
source_name: Han et al. 2015

description: There are no Korean symptom data or occurrence records on maize. EPPO lists Korea as "Present, few occurrences", but the basis is a single 2010 detection on *Dracaena sanderiana* in a greenhouse in Gyeonggi.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, ERWIST distribution KR

description: Susceptible sweet corn hybrids wilt quickly (wilt phase). Dent hybrids are generally resistant to the wilt phase. Plants die at the seedling stage, or if infected late may grow to some extent.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Sweet corn infected early is most severely affected. Young plants wilt, are stunted, and show water-soaked lesions with wavy margins.
source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)
location_in_source: End of p.2 Injury paragraph (sweet corn)

description: Sweet corn: pale green to yellow longitudinal streaks with irregular or wavy margins that can run the full length of the leaf. Streaks turn brown as they dry.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Dent corn: short or long irregular pale green to yellow streaks **starting from flea beetle feeding scars**. Diseased areas, sometimes whole leaves, turn straw-colored.
short_quote: "start at corn flea beetle feeding marks"
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Lesions start at feeding scars (small scratches). They are pale green to yellow streaks at first and turn brown as tissue dies. Margins are usually wavy but follow the veins overall. The photo description mentions water-soaked wavy margins.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, Stewart's Disease of Corn (posted 2026-09-24) (CPN-Stewart)
location_in_source: Body symptom paragraph and photo descriptions

description: Severely infected plants may develop **cavities in the stalk pith near the soil line**. Weakened plants are more prone to stalk rot.
short_quote: "Cavities may form in the stalk pith"
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: When the stalk is infected the whole plant wilts.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, Stewart's Disease of Corn (posted 2026-09-24) (CPN-Stewart)

description: Tassels emerge early, bleach, and wilt and die before the rest of the plant. Small irregular water-soaked spots form inside and outside the husks and darken as they dry. Small droplets of exudate may form on inner husks.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Drought worsens the disease. As a result ears are often small or absent.
short_quote: "small ears or no ears at all"
source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)

description: Bacteria penetrate deep into the seed but do not reach the embryo. Dent corn kernels are rarely infected unless disease is severe and the hybrid susceptible.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: When an infected stalk or leaf is cut across, **masses of yellow bacterial slime** emerge.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Viewing a lesion section at about ×100 or more shows bacteria streaming (ooze) from the vascular bundles.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: When an infected stalk is cut, **pale yellow bacterial droplets** may seep out.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, Stewart's Disease of Corn (posted 2026-09-24) (CPN-Stewart)

description: Adults spread the bacteria while feeding. Bacteria accumulate in and block the vascular bundles, interfering with water and nutrient movement. Infection can occur at any time during growth, and there are two phases: seedling infection (wilt phase) and infection after tasseling (leaf blight phase). Most commercial field corn is resistant to the wilt phase but somewhat susceptible to the leaf blight phase.
source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)

description: Seedlings are mainly infected by vector feeding, and secondary spread occurs during summer.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Field corn shows few symptoms until late summer, after which many leaf lesions form. In years with many flea beetles, some hybrids wilt and die before tasseling. Under suitable conditions, almost 100% of susceptible field corn hybrids show symptoms by late autumn.
source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)

description: Leaf streaks on dent corn usually appear after tasseling.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: If the mean daily temperature in December–February is above freezing, vectors survive and severe disease is possible. Below −3 °C, survival is unlikely and severe disease is unlikely.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Non-motile, non-spore-forming, **Gram-negative rods**, 0.4–0.7 × 0.9–2.0 µm, occurring singly or in short chains.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: On nutrient-glucose agar, colonies are cream-yellow, lemon-yellow or orange-yellow, and flat, raised or convex.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: EPPO diagnostic protocol **PM 7/60(2)** covers isolation, immunofluorescence (IF), ELISA, molecular tests (conventional and real-time PCR, barcoding) and fatty acid analysis. The USA recommends ELISA-based testing of maize seed lots. The PM 7/60 text itself could not be opened.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Adults: small, shiny black, about 1/16 inch (≈1.6 mm, converted), with thick hind legs, good jumpers. Larvae: small, white and not very active. Mature larvae are 1/6 inch (≈4.2 mm, converted), with only the prothorax and last abdominal segment slightly darker.
source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)

description: Scrapes the upper and lower leaf epidermis, leaving **scratches usually parallel to the veins (windowpane)**. Does not chew through the leaf. Heavily fed leaves look white or silvery. Leaves can be covered with feeding scars when new adults emerge in June and August.
source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)

description: Overwinters as adults in soil and debris along fencerows, roadsides and woodland edges. Becomes active at 65–70 °F (≈18–21 °C, converted). One generation takes about a month, with first-generation adults in June and second-generation adults in early August. A third generation may occur in southern Illinois. Seen first at field edges.
source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)

description: The main US vector is *C. pulicaria*. Adults overwinter and carry the bacteria in the gut for life. They can travel long distances on air currents. Vector morphology is not described.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Goss's wilt can look very similar. *Acidovorax avenae*: long narrow streaks with reddish-brown margins, leaf shredding. *Burkholderia andropogonis*: long narrow parallel olive-green to yellow water-soaked lesions. Northern corn leaf blight: large spindle-shaped gray-green to tan spots. Southern corn leaf blight and *C. carbonum*: well-defined tan to brown spots.
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

description: Both Goss's and Stewart's diseases cause seedling blight and long lesions with wavy margins between veins. The distinguishing feature is the dark green to black freckles of Goss's. Stewart's has been rarely recorded since the early 2000s.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)
location_in_source: Diseases and Other Conditions with Similar Symptoms > Stewart's

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Korean source: Unconfirmed. The EPPO distribution table has no entry for Korea or Asia. This does not confirm absence. The EPPO web datasheet showed only Identity and distribution; the symptom and morphology sections could not be viewed.
source_name: EPPO CORBNE

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Young lesions are light green water-soaked streaks with gray-green margins. When mature they become long tan to gray-brown lesions with irregular or wavy margins parallel to the veins. They often start at the leaf tip or at hail or sandblasting wounds. When lesions merge, more than 60% of the leaf area can die.
short_quote: "streaks of light green tissue with water-soaking"
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Long, large tan lesions form in the middle or along the margin of the leaf. Margins may look water-soaked.
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Within lesions there are scattered, discontinuous dark green to black water-soaked spots (freckles). They look translucent against the light and are diagnostic of Goss's.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: The black spots (freckles) within lesions can be large and **do not rub off**. They are mainly at lesion margins but may be scattered throughout the lesion.
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Freckles form near the margins of expanding lesions.
source_name: Univ. of Nebraska–Lincoln CropWatch, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight (UNL-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Under humid conditions small orange droplets of bacterial exudate form on lesions. Dried exudate shines like dried varnish.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Exudate is visible on lesion surfaces in the early morning or after rain. Dried exudate is glossy, especially in direct sunlight.
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Bacteria produce exudate on the leaf surface, which shines like varnish when dry.
source_name: Univ. of Nebraska–Lincoln CropWatch, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight (UNL-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Bacteria streaming from lesion sections (bacterial streaming) can be seen under the microscope.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Xylem discoloration or slimy stalk rot develops, leading through wilting to death. Figure 6 shows 'discolored stalk pith'. The discoloration color is not described.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Stalk vascular bundles **discolor orange to brown** because the bacteria move within the xylem.
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: As bacteria infect and move through the vascular bundles, the xylem discolors, and eventually the plant wilts and dies of slimy stalk rot. Color is not described.
source_name: Univ. of Nebraska–Lincoln CropWatch, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight (UNL-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Plants with the wilt phase show drought-stress symptoms and wilt or die early.
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Plants infected late wilt as if from drought, and weakened stalks lodge easily.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Infection can occur at any growth stage. Infection before V6 usually becomes systemic, causing death and stand loss, and systemic wilt is often first seen at V2–V6. Infection after V6 becomes leaf blight. Symptoms are most distinct and severe after silking (R1). Infection during the vegetative stage can reduce yield by more than 50%.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Enters any part of the plant through hail or strong-wind wounds and spreads by windblown rain. It can also enter through insect feeding wounds, but insects do not transmit it. Hot, dry weather slows progression, making it hard to distinguish from drought.
short_quote: "insects are not known to transmit the bacteria"
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Seed-to-seedling transmission is low at about 2%, but infected seed can introduce the disease to new areas.
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Transmitted by seed, but seedling transmission is low so it is not regarded as a main source of infection. Infected residue on the soil surface is the main inoculum.
source_name: Univ. of Nebraska–Lincoln CropWatch, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight (UNL-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: A **Gram-positive bacterium** (one of the few plant diseases caused by Gram-positive bacteria). Cell size and colony color are not given in this source.
source_name: Univ. of Nebraska–Lincoln CropWatch, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight (UNL-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: For confirmation, send samples for diagnostic lab testing including microscopy, isolation and serological tests.
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Northern corn leaf blight lesions are canoe- or cigar-shaped, 1–4 inches (≈2.5–10 cm, converted) long and 1/2–1 inch wide. Early margins are gray-green, and mature lesions are tan with dark sporulation. Margins are even, with no freckles or streaming. On some hybrids margin discoloration can look like freckles.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: *X. vasicola* pv. *vasculorum*: narrower tan to yellow lesions than Goss's, from under 1 inch to several inches long, bright yellow against the light. No freckles; streaming can occur in both diseases.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus deficiencies lack water-soaked freckles, glossy exudate and streaming. Drought and leaf scorch usually progress inward from the leaf margin, are more uniform in color, and lack those three features.
source_name: Crop Protection Network, An Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight (CPN-Goss)

disease: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight
description: Leaf blight is easily confused with drought or chemical leaf scorch in dry weather. It can also be misdiagnosed as nutrient deficiency, chemical injury, Stewart's disease or northern corn leaf blight.
source_name: Wise, Ruhl, Creswell, Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight, Purdue Ext. BP-81-W (2010-05) (Purdue-BP81)

description: Korean source: Unconfirmed. Korea is not among the Asian entries of the EPPO distribution table (Guangxi China, India, Indonesia, Nepal, Pakistan, Philippines, Thailand). Only Identity and distribution of the EPPO web datasheet could be viewed.
source_name: EPPO-PRSCPH

description: The first symptoms appear as chlorotic streaks on the first leaves as early as **9 days after sowing**.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Long chlorotic (yellow) streaks may appear on all leaves of a plant. Heavily infected cells collapse and chloroplasts are destroyed, giving a yellow color (Weston 1920).
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Distinct green and yellow streaks form on leaves, and a gray to white downy coating may grow on the leaf surface.
source_name: USDA CAPS datasheet *P. philippinensis* Version 2 (2021-09-29) (CAPS-Pp-2021)

description: Chlorosis spreads widely and white downy masses form on the leaf underside. Ear development is delayed or poor.
short_quote: "white downy mass on the ventral leaf surface"
source_name: Singh J., "Relative disease reaction of maize varieties to downy mildews over varied environments (IDMN 1969–1973)", Tropical Agriculture Research Series No. 8, pp.129–152 (JIRCAS publication; **publication year unconfirmed in the original**) (Singh-TARS8)

description: A gray downy coating (conidia on conidiophores) forms mainly on the leaf underside. It is visible **from the 2-leaf stage until tassels and silks emerge** and is a source of secondary spread.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Conidiophores emerge from stomata in chlorotic areas on both leaf surfaces (more on the underside, where stomata are more numerous). They also emerge from leaf sheaths, the tassel axis, glumes and husks.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Sporulation begins around midnight and continues until the surface dries. After 1–2 hours of exposure to sunlight, wind or low humidity, conidia shrivel. Conidia are sparse the morning after the first symptoms and abundant after systemic symptoms.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Grayish-white down is present on chlorotic areas but may dry from sunlight or low humidity, leaving only 'matted patches'.
source_name: USDA CAPS Small Grains manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (Table 1, citing White 1999) (CAPS-Pp-SG)

description: From the seedling, yellow streaks enlarge on successively higher leaves (a scouting point).
short_quote: "larger and larger yellow streaks on succeeding leaves"
source_name: USDA CAPS Small Grains manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (Table 1, citing White 1999) (CAPS-Pp-SG)

description: Mycelium spreads between mesophyll cells, moves down the leaf sheath, passes through the stalk and establishes in the growing point. Once the meristem is invaded, chlorotic streaks soon form and spores are produced there. The fungus is present only in chlorotic, not green, areas.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: As plants grow, leaves become narrow, abnormally upright and look dry.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: At maturity tassels become malformed with reduced pollen, ear formation stops, and seed may be sterile. Early infection causes stunting or death.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn); USDA CAPS datasheet *P. philippinensis* Version 2 (2021-09-29) (CAPS-Pp-2021)

description: Seeds show no external symptoms. Mycelium is in the pericarp and also in the embryo and endosperm.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Sugarcane: the bases of young leaves turn white, and old leaves show mosaic or mottling and then turn brick-red. Stalks become thin.
source_name: USDA CAPS datasheet *P. philippinensis* Version 2 (2021-09-29) (CAPS-Pp-2021)

description: Conidia are produced at 18–23 °C and germinate at 10–35 °C. Infection is highest above 16 °C. Night temperatures of 21–26 °C are needed for conidial production, germination and infection. A water film on the leaf surface in darkness for at least 4–5 hours is required.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: An obligate biotroph that does not grow on artificial media. Hyphae are branched and slender (8 µm diameter), irregularly constricted or swollen. Conidiophores are erect, **15–26 × 150–400 µm**, emerge from stomata and **branch dichotomously 2–4 times** with stout branches. Sterigmata are ovoid to subulate, slightly curved, 10 µm long. Conidia are **17–21 × 27–39 µm**, elongate-ovoid to rounded cylindrical, hyaline, with slightly rounded tips. Haustoria are simple vesicular to digitate, 8 × 2 µm.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Oospores are rare and not produced in maize tissue. When produced they are globose, smooth-walled, about 22 µm in diameter, germinating by a lateral germ tube.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Table 1 (White 1999): ***P. philippinensis*** conidiophores 150–400 µm, swollen and abruptly widening, 2–4 dichotomous branchings, ephemeral; conidia 17–21 × 27–39 µm; oospores rare or absent, 22.6 µm. ***P. maydis*** conidiophores 150–550 µm; conidia globose to subglobose 17–23 × 27–39 µm; oospores unknown. ***P. sacchari*** conidiophores 160–170 µm, gradually widening, 2–3 branchings; conidia elliptical, oblong or conical '15-239' (apparently a misprint) × 25–41 µm; oospores yellow to yellow-brown 40–50 µm. ***P. sorghi*** conidiophores 180–300 µm, 2–3 branchings, septum near the base; conidia elliptical to nearly globose 15–26.9 × 15–28.9 µm; oospores usually brown 25–42.9 µm. All *Peronosclerospora* conidia germinate by a **germ tube**.
source_name: USDA CAPS Small Grains manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (Table 1, citing White 1999) (CAPS-Pp-SG)

description: Morphological characters vary greatly with culture conditions, developmental stage and host. *Peronosclerospora* is divided by conidial shape into three groups (globose / ovoid to slightly elongate / long or slipper-shaped), but differences within groups are small.
source_name: USDA CAPS Corn manual datasheet, *P. philippinensis* (CAPS-Pp-corn)

description: Downy mildew fungi are distinguished only by fine morphological differences, so definitive identification is difficult. Conidiophores may exist for only a few hours, and morphology is affected by environment and host. Eleven downy mildew species in 3 genera have been reported on maize.
source_name: Groben G. et al. 2026, Fungal Syst. Evol. 17:221–232 (CC BY 4.0) (Groben2026)
